source_document.body:
Every career has a story. In Leadership Lessons , supply chain leaders reflect on the experiences that shaped who they are and how they lead.
Long before Jonathan Scherr was helping lead a supply chain technology company, he spent Saturday nights as an event DJ outside Boston, working weddings and bar mitzvahs.
The job meant walking into a room full of strangers and helping them celebrate. When something went wrong, he had to stay upbeat and fix it fast.
More Leadership Lessons
Lindsay Azim, Gartner
Steve Liou, CEO of Clarium
Jackie Wu, Corvus Robotics
Peter Bollinger, CEO of EPG
Peter Bennett, Cardinal Health
View all Leadership Lessons stories
“As a first job it was a crash course on thinking on my feet. Constantly had to read a room, course correct when things weren't working, and deal with people when emotions were running high.”
Now chief strategy and operations officer at project44 , Scherr works to bring the same optimism and solution orientation to some of the most complex problems facing customers and their supply chain operations. Another principle guides how he leads: “Just show up is a pretty powerful thesis, first and foremost.”
Being there for people has followed him through a career spanning finance, education , technology , and housing. Along the way, he has learned that showing up also means taking responsibility, especially when something goes wrong.
Curiosity starts at home
Scherr grew up in Newton, Massachusetts, the younger of two brothers. His mother spent decades working in Boston public schools as a speech and language pathologist, while his father moved from education into construction and real estate.
Education mattered at home, but so did asking questions. Dinner conversations encouraged the brothers to discuss what they had learned and keep asking why.
Scherr loved musical theater, played sports, and became editor-in-chief of his high school newspaper.
At Dartmouth, he initially thought he would become a doctor, following in the footsteps of an uncle who was a surgeon. During the college’s shopping period, he sat in on the first organic chemistry class and walked out within 30 minutes.
An introductory economics class offered something more appealing: a way to study why people make decisions. He became especially interested in development economics and how household choices could improve someone’s financial prospects or keep a family in poverty.
It laid the foundation for a deep interest in using data to understand the world differently and shed light on how organizations should operate to do things better. Everything he's focused on since has been grounded in that foundation
At 20, he took a semester off to work with a nonprofit in Tanzania providing care to people with HIV and AIDS. Drawing on emergency medical training from Dartmouth’s ski patrol, he helped with home-based health care and hospice work.
The experience brought his studies to life. It also led him to question nonprofits as a way to address those problems, given the waste and inefficiency he observed.

Leaving the comfortable path
Scherr’s early finance work included commercial mortgage-backed securities at Morgan Stanley as the mortgage crisis was beginning. He later worked in private equity, investing in software and technology businesses. His first investment assignment involved Accellos, a supply chain software company that later merged with HighJump, giving him an early connection to the industry he would eventually return to at project44.
He could see a comfortable career ahead. Then an episode of The Colbert Report sent him in another direction.
A Harvard economist appeared on the show to discuss research on improving outcomes in high-poverty U.S. communities, particularly through education. Scherr reached out and eventually left finance to work alongside him, helping turn the research into a nonprofit that works with schools.
Scherr helped found Blueprint Schools Network as its chief operating officer. The work connected his interest in data with education issues he had heard his mother discuss for years and introduced him to personalized learning.
He went on to Harvard Business School and the Harvard Kennedy School, advised education technology company AltSchool, and worked at financial technology company CircleUp. Later, he co-founded and led Juno, which sought to simplify how housing was designed and built.
At Juno, Scherr teamed up with a former Apple executive who spent about 20 years as the company's chief architect for its stores. The aim was to make building housing more repeatable, with consistent components and a simpler process for bringing a project from design to construction.
It meant working well beyond software. Components had to be designed and sourced , so the team had to build a supply chain around them. They also had to work with contractors and arrange financing through lenders and investors.
“It’s a fundamentally different puzzle than just writing software,” he says. For Scherr, the appeal was tackling a practical problem that could improve access to housing.
“I want my team to be 1% better every day because the compounding of that is massive.”
Across education, technology, and housing, Scherr kept returning to the same idea of how data could help solve complicated, real-world problems. While the industries changed, his interest in turning information into better decisions remained constant. That thinking eventually drew him to project44, where years of accumulated supply chain data created an entirely new opportunity with AI . Scherr began advising project44 in August 2017 and took a more hands-on role in fall 2024, before becoming chief strategy and operations officer in March 2025.
“I was very much excited about a business that didn’t exist yet,” Scherr says, recalling his initial involvement in 2017. The company was building connections between sources of supply chain information, and he believed the data it gathered could become the basis for something much bigger.
By 2024, he felt that opportunity had arrived. After years of building a vast supply chain data network, project44 was positioned to capitalize on advances in AI. Scherr stepped into a more active leadership role with a central mandate: accelerate the company’s AI strategy and turn its data advantage into technology that could help customers make better supply chain decisions.
That focus helped shape project44’s evolution toward using AI to help customers anticipate disruptions , use insights, make decisions and take action.
Today, Scherr says, companies with complex supply chain challenges use project44’s platform to reduce friction and bias in their work. Its data foundation gives customers reliable information for AI, whether they use project44’s agentic platform or draw on its data for AI applications elsewhere.
Responsibility moves up
Scherr’s “just show up” approach to leadership means frequent travel to meet with project44’s global team, customers and prospective customers. At the time of the interview, he had traveled to India nine times to meet colleagues in Bangalore, often for just two or three days. He says the office has more than 250 people, roughly half the company’s headcount, so time there is important for understanding and developing the team and ensuring the company delivers on its promises to customers.
“It’s really powerful when you show up,” he says of spending time with that team. With two young children at home, the travel also requires him to be especially present when he returns.
He keeps a sign beside his desk that reads “1% better.” It reminds him to consider each day how he and his team have improved as people, contributors or teammates.
“I want my team to be 1% better every day because the compounding of that is massive,” he says. His point is that small daily gains build on one another, while small declines accumulate in the other direction.
Another expectation is more pointed: “Never be as surprised as me.” When a direct report brings him an issue and says, “I’m as surprised as you,” Scherr responds, “You don’t get to be.”
Surprises happen when a company moves quickly, but managers should understand and take responsibility for their areas. He holds himself to the same standard as the CEO. For Scherr, wins are earned by the front lines, while losses are owned at the top.
That means owning decisions and outcomes rather than blaming a junior employee when something is missed. Managers have a responsibility to protect their teams, with accountability moving up through the organization.
The same principle applies to customers. Showing up means being available when an implementation gets complicated or something goes wrong, then helping work through the problem.
For Scherr, giving employees credit for success comes with a responsibility to stand behind them when things go wrong.
“It’s very much about true ownership that rolls up, not down.”
